Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

text:
The Rolling Stone photo used to kill interest in ivermectin showed people in winter coats waiting for flu shots in July.

Joe Rogan and Peter McCullough walked through the sequence: the Oklahoma ER line that turned out to be a flu-shot queue, the FDA’s “You’re not a horse” campaign, and the subsequent lawsuit by critical-care doctors (including Paul Marik, Mary Talley Bowden, and others) that forced the agency to take the messaging down.

What McCullough highlighted from the Ron Johnson hearing is the data point that rarely gets airtime. Attorney Ralph Lorigo secured court orders for ivermectin in 62 hospital cases; those patients lived. In the cases where the order was denied or blocked, the outcomes were uniformly fatal. Lorigo was explicit that this is not a randomized trial, just the pattern that emerged when families had to litigate for access. McCullough has testified under oath that he believes ~85% of the deaths were avoidable with the multi-drug protocols (ivermectin + steroids + the rest of the outpatient stack) he published earlier.

The part that still doesn’t have a clean explanation is the speed and uniformity of the pushback. Australia, Europe, India, and U.S. institutions all moved in the same direction within a very short window, even after early observational signals appeared. That level of coordination usually has a structural cause, liability in liability, reimbursement rules, or messaging guidelines, rather than pure scientific disagreement.

Curious where people land on the institutional piece. If the early data was weak enough to justify the campaign, why did the same suppression pattern hold in places that never had the same regulatory incentives?

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
Open Letter to @Meta , @finkd , @mosseri @instagram @kunalb11  @facebook @WhatsApp , and Everyone Watching

@Meta ,

You built platforms that hold our memories, our businesses, our friendships, our work. Then you handed the keys to AI and walked away.

Accounts on Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp are being disabled or suspended overnight by automated systems. No clear reason. No warning. No human in the loop. Just a bot decision that can erase years of life in seconds.

Sometimes you send an email later saying “we made a mistake, you can use the account again.” Then nothing changes. The account stays locked. Or worse while it’s locked in appeal, it gets compromised. Unauthorized recovery numbers appear. Hidden apps show up. Codes stop working. And the person who built that account for a decade is left staring at recovery screens that keep changing.

When accounts finally come back, if they come back at all, it’s often just a quiet “sorry.” No explanation. No accountability.

PUBLIC LEGAL NOTICE

Date: 25th July 2026 

TO:
1. THE UNIDENTIFIED INDIVIDUAL (JANE DOE) 
Featured in Subject Instagram Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)

2. THE GRIEVANCE OFFICER & LEGAL CELL
  Meta Platforms, Inc. / Instagram LLC
  (Intermediary hosting subject digital broadcast)

3. TO WHOMSOEVER IT MAY CONCERN / GENERAL PUBLIC
SUBJECT: LEGAL NOTICE DEMANDING CEASE & DESIST, IMMEDIATE TAKEDOWN OF UNLAWFUL DIGITAL CONTENT, PUBLIC RETRACTION, AND INITIATION OF PROCEEDINGS UNDER THE BHARATIYA NYAYA SANHITA (BNS), 2023 AND THE INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY ACT, 2000.

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

1.1 THAT in the aforementioned video broadcast, you have publicly uttered, performed, and disseminated statements/actions that are defamatory, inciting public mischief, & outraging public sentiments , hereby causing grave injury to public peace .

2. Your acts and public utterances attract strict criminal liability under BNS, 2023, specifically under:
   a) Section 351 (Criminal Intimidation);
   b) Section 353 (Public Mischief & Incitement to commit offenses against public tranquility);
   c) Section 356 (Defamation & Damage to Reputation);
   d) Section 299 / 196 (Outraging religious sentiments / Promoting enmity between classes, if applicable).

2.1 The electronic transmission and public hosting of the impugned content violates Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, imposing a mandatory duty on platform intermediaries to disable access to objectionable digital material.

In light of the statutory breaches detailed above, you are hereby called upon to comply with the following requisites within SEVEN (7) DAYS from the date of this Notice:
A. CEASE AND DESIST- Immediately cease and desist from making, publishing, or propagating similar illegal, inflammatory, or defamatory statements/videos across any digital medium.

B. TAKEDOWN AND DELETION - Ensure the immediate deletion and permanent takedown of the impugned Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)from Instagram and all mirror platforms.

C. PUBLIC APOLOGY / RETRACTION- Issue an unconditional public apology across official digital channels acknowledging the improper nature of the broadcast and expressing regret.
 
TAKE NOTICE that if you fail to strictly comply with the terms of this Legal Notice within the stipulated period of 7 (Seven) days, it shall be constrained to initiate appropriate civil and criminal proceedings against you—including filing a formal First Information Report (FIR) under the relevant provisions of BNS, 2023 read with Section 66 of the IT Act, 2000, alongside seeking direction from the competent Judicial Magistrate under Section 175(3) of BNSS, 2023—entirely at your risk, cost, and legal consequences.
 
A copy of this Notice is retained in my office for future legal records and evidentiary reliance under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023.

Shruti Dixit
Advocate
Rajasthan High Court

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

RAG vs. Graph RAG vs. Agentic RAG, clearly explained!

Standard RAG embeds documents into vectors and retrieves the most similar chunks via similarity search. For direct factual lookups, this works well.

But it breaks down when a query needs to connect facts spread across multiple documents. Similarity search retrieves individual chunks, not the relationships between them.

Graph RAG adds a knowledge graph layer on top.

→ During indexing, an LLM extracts entities and relationships from the documents.

→ During retrieval, the system traverses these connections instead of relying on embedding similarity alone.

This is what enables multi-hop queries.

Say a vector DB stores three facts about internal services:

↳ "The checkout service uses payments API."
↳ "The payments API runs on cluster-3."
↳ "Cluster-3 is scheduled for maintenance on Friday."

Someone asks: "Will the checkout service be affected by Friday's maintenance?"

Vector search can likely retrieve facts 1 and 3 because the query mentions "checkout service" and "Friday maintenance."

But it will miss fact 2, which connects the payments API to cluster-3.

That middle fact sits too far from the query in embedding space. It mentions neither "checkout" nor "maintenance," so it never makes it into the retrieved context.

A knowledge graph connects these as linked entities, and graph traversal finds the full path in one query.

Agentic RAG takes a different approach entirely.

Instead of a fixed retrieval pipeline, an LLM agent decides at query time which tools to invoke, which sources to query, and in what order.

Check the visual below to understand the three architectures thoroughly.

One thing to note here is that these three aren't levels of sophistication that you need to graduate through.

Instead, they solve different query types.

↳ Single-hop factual lookups → standard RAG
↳ Multi-hop relationship queries → Graph RAG
↳ Dynamic multi-source tasks with tool use → Agentic RAG

Once the right architecture is in place, the next leverage point is efficiency.

Most RAG architectures rely heavily on vector search, and that layer can be made 32x more memory-efficient using binary quantization.

1. The topic, as one line: "everything you need to know about ___ before you ___ (play, buy, watch, visit, file, switch)". If I have none, pitch me 3 that launch or peak in the next 30 days and tell me the date for each.
2. The viewer: who they are and what they are about to do.
3. The length: a 60-90 s sample, 5 minutes, or the full 20-35 minutes.
4. The voice: an ElevenLabs voice id and key if I have them, otherwise a free local voice. If it is paid, tell me the character count (about 1 credit each) and wait for my yes.
5. Any footage I already have, and any source I do not want used.
6. The two colours for the gradient, or let you pick them from the subject's key art.
Everything is researched fresh on the day. Never copy another video's script, order or jokes.
</inputs>

<direction>
A faceless 1920x1080, 30 fps explainer built entirely on real moving footage of the subject: official trailers, gameplay reveals, launch films, keynote clips, press b-roll, archive film. About 90% of the picture is that footage. There is no face-cam, no talking head, no AI-generated plate and no stock clip that is not the subject.
The picture changes about every 2 seconds, always with hard cuts, at the same rate from the first second to the last. Every concrete thing the voice names gets proof on screen inside half a second: a rounded glass card holding a photo, a real headline screenshot, a character panel, a typed quote or one big number. While a card is up, the footage keeps running behind it, blurred 26 px and darkened 40-60%.
One look for every graphic: dark plum glass #1E1322, a thin pale-pink border #F7D3EA with a soft pink glow (255,120,205), Montserrat Black in uppercase, and a left-to-right gradient #FF93DC to #FFB27C on captions, chapter words, numbers and names. Source pills are pink #FB96E6, cream #FFF1DE or peach #FFBA90 with dark caps. If the subject is not warm and neon, take two neighbouring hues from its key art and keep the panels near-black in the same hue.
The voice is fast, flat and plain. It says "you" constantly, marks every opinion as one, and names where each fact came from.
Banned: a greeting, a channel or narrator name, "in today's video", "let's dive in", a recap of what was just said, "thanks for watching", dissolves between shots, a subtitle for every word, a sound effect on cuts or text, music loud enough to notice, any shot shown twice, any shot over 6 s, a card over a face, a mock-up shown as a real screenshot, a leak used as evidence, and any fact with no named source.
</direction>

<structure>
Length and pace: 205-215 words a minute. 60-90 s is about 210-320 words; 5 minutes is about 1,050; 20 minutes is 4,300; 30 minutes is 6,400. The picture changes about 28 times a minute, 24-29 times in the first 60 s.
The shape: line 1 is a fact about the subject or a "you" line about the viewer's habit, with the first concrete fact inside 10 seconds → an intro of 30-65 s (110-230 words) holding one stakes line about the viewer, one scope promise ("everything" or a number), 3-6 teaser facts of one clause each, one trust line ("I checked every single thing") and one promise parked "at the very end" → a handoff of under 8 words that names section 1 → sections of 2:10-2:40 each (none under 0:55, none over 4:15; 10-13 of them in a full video, 2 in a 5-minute cut), ordered as a chain so each bridge can truthfully say "you now have X, so Y" → inside a section: open on old way vs new way or a one-word label, put the biggest change first, flag the most important item out loud in the middle ("and this is the big one"), end long sections with three actions in one sentence, then a 1-2 sentence bridge that states the next topic as a problem → every intro teaser is paid off later with a spoken callback ("remember the ___ from the start?"), never two payoffs in one section, the last one in the final 10% → the end promise is teased again between 20% and 40% of the way through → one subscribe ask between 30% and 50%, 2-4 sentences, joined by "because" to a tease of the next section → the close, under 60 s: a personal plan in three steps, "here's my hot take" in 3-4 sentences, "but you tell me" with an either/or question, then one sign-off line.
The fact unit, repeated every 15-25 s (about 57 words, 16 s): the claim in 1-2 sentences of 15 words or fewer → the named source in the same or next sentence ("X told Y", "X says", "you can see it in the trailer") → a confidence label if it is not official ("only X has reported it", "the reports don't agree yet", "nobody has shown that", "busted") → a line starting with "So" that says what you do, avoid or check → sometimes one joke, always after the fact, never two in a row.
The voice rules: sentences average 12-14 words, at least 28% of them 8 words or fewer, none over 50. At least 72% one-syllable words. "You" or "your" at least 8 times a minute, "I" 2-4 times, "we" almost never. 30-40% of sentences start with "And" or "So". A named source at least every 20 s, never 85 s without one. A "So" line at least every 30 s. Round every number with "about", say units the way people say them, and follow a big number with something the viewer knows ("about 210 gigs, a third of your console's drive"). Pick one piece of advice as the motif and say it at least 4 times, including in the last line.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools (all free, all local). Install what's missing and tell me what you installed:
   - Python 3.10+ with numpy and Pillow, FFmpeg with ffprobe, yt-dlp
   - Playwright with Chromium, for headline screenshots and for drawing the graphics layer
   - faster-whisper with large-v3-turbo, int8 on the CPU, for word timings
   - Montserrat Black and Bold (free licence)
   - Kokoro (kokoro-onnx) for the free voice, or my ElevenLabs key read from a file and never printed
   - One project folder per video: research, script, a media folder with a source list, the voice, the timeline, the renders
2. Research, before any writing:
   - Search the web and open the pages. Nothing from memory.
   - For each fact keep the claim, the page, the exact words it rests on, the date and the confidence: official, on-record interview, seen by a previewer, single source, sources disagree, estimate, unknown, false.
   - Prefer the maker's own pages, then on-record interviews, then named outlets. Check every fact against a second source and drop what you cannot confirm.
   - You need one usable fact per 16 s of film, so about 19 for 5 minutes.
3. Script, then a check you run on it:
   - Write one sentence per line under section headings, and mark each teaser, payoff, joke, flag and the ask.
   - Write a small checker and run it until it passes: first fact inside 10 s, intro 30-65 s, every teaser paid off, mean sentence length 12-14 words, a named source every 20 s, "you" 8 times a minute, words per minute, one ask between 30% and 50%, none of the banned phrases.
   - Write out how the voice should say anything it will get wrong: product names, numbers, places ("212" as "two hundred and twelve").
   - Show me the script, the source list and the checker's result before you record.
4. Voice and timing:
   - Record one take per section, not per sentence: it flows better.
   - Transcribe each take with faster-whisper and match its words to the script with difflib. Take every time from that match, never from the voice service's own timestamps, which drift up to 0.4 s late on long takes.
   - List every word that was heard differently from the script. A name spelled another way is fine. A wrong word means redoing that one section only.
   - Cut silences down to 0.30 s, and only inside real silence (under -35 dB), keeping 35 ms either side. Then, if the pace is still under 205 wpm, speed up by at most 1.12x and stop there, even if it lands lower.
   - Level with a light compressor and two-pass loudnorm to -18 LUFS, loudness range 3 LU or less, true peak under -2 dB.
5. Media, with every file's page, link and date saved in one source list:
   - Footage: list the search results first and take the maker's own upload, never a re-upload with someone's watermark. 2-4 sources per 10 minutes of film.
   - Split each source into scenes with FFmpeg's scene score, make a numbered sheet of them, and look at it. Drop logos, title cards, rating boards, "presents" plates, burned-in dates and anything intimate or graphic.
   - Count the shots: you need about 25 different ones per minute. If you are short, add official stills as full-frame shots, 2.8 s each with a 3% push-in over 2.5 s, but keep them under about 10% of the runtime.
   - Crop letterboxed sources to fill the frame.
   - Headlines: screenshot the headline alone on the page's own background with Playwright. If the crop is not clean, set the headline as text on white with the outlet and the date.
   - Photos: the page's main image, free-licence sources first (the maker's press kit, Wikimedia Commons, NASA).
6. Timeline and graphics, every time keyed to a word in the script, never to a fixed second:
   - Footage: cut every 1.7-3.7 s (aim for 2.6 s), alternating bright and dark scenes. Wherever the voice names something you can see, pin that exact shot under the word. Cut mid-sentence, not on pauses.
   - Cards start 0.12 s before their word and fade in and out over 0.25 s. Holds: photo 2.6 s, headline 2.8 s, character 2.8 s, number 1.5 s, quote until 0.9 s after its last word. A card needs at least 1.2 s on screen. Aim for a card up 35-40% of the runtime.
   - Photo card: the image keeps its own shape, up to 44% of the frame wide (portrait up to 30% wide and 74% tall), tilted 1.4°, with a name pill on its lower-left corner, footage behind darkened 42%.
   - Headline card: 50% of the frame wide, tilted 1.1°, the outlet as a pill on its top-left corner, footage behind darkened 50%.
   - Character card: a 474x896 portrait panel at x 64.5% (or 10.5% on the left), photo on top, name in the gradient, two lines under it, over sharp footage with no darkening.
   - Quote card: from x 19% to 81% with its top at y 54%, a pink opening mark, the words typed one by one with the voice in white, then a pink attribution pill, footage behind darkened 55%.
   - Number card: one gradient figure 250 px tall, shrunk to fit 80% of the width, with a small spaced line under it.
   - Captions: only the 1-6 key words of a sentence, centred at y 80%, wrapped at 60% of the width. 116 px for 1-2 words, 106 px for 3, 92 px for 4-5, 80 px for 6. Each word fades in over 0.2 s on the moment it is spoken, the layout never shifts, and the phrase is gone at the next cut or 0.6 s after its last word. One about every 6-7 s in the intro and every 8-10 s later.
   - Chapter words: 1-3 words at 214 px, shrunk to fit 72% of the width, held 2 s over footage blurred and darkened 60%. One per section.
   - Source pills: 27 px caps, tilted a few degrees, stacked from the top-left corner (66 px in, 52 px down, 76 px apart), one the first time each source is named in a section. Use them for confidence too: REPORTED, ESTIMATE, BUSTED.
   - Never more than 5 s of bare footage in the first minute, or 7 s after it.
   - Draw all of this as one transparent HTML page, export it frame by frame with Playwright, and lay it over the footage in FFmpeg, switching the blur on and off on the exact frames a card starts and ends.
7. Render, measure and look:
   - Before any render, draw every shot in film order with its caption written on it, and read all of them. Fix every caption that sits on the wrong picture.
   - Render a 960x540 preview first. Pull 4 frames a second from the first minute and from two 30 s windows later, and read every sheet: cards on their word, captions building with the voice, no card over a face, nothing bare for too long.
   - Look at one full-size frame of each card type and fix the finish: border weight, glow, corner radius, type size, blur depth.
   - Render 1080p, then measure and show me the numbers next to these targets: 25-31 picture changes a minute, median shot 1.9-2.4 s, 3% or fewer shots over 6 s, a card up 35-40% of the time, stills under 10%, longest pause 0.5 s, -18 LUFS, voice and captions within 50 ms of each other at the end of the film.
   - Do at least three look-and-fix rounds, then give me the film, a phone copy under 25 MB, a credits list of every source, and an honest list of what still falls short.
</build>

<gotchas>
- A trailer is cut for mood, so its best shots are often the wrong picture for a factual line. Check every caption against the shot under it, or "in-game purchases" ends up over a love scene.
- A slower narrator makes the film longer, which empties the footage pool. Add shots or stills. Never let a shot come round twice.
- Stills creep up when footage is short. Past 10% of the runtime the film starts to feel like a slideshow.
- Voice services return word timestamps that drift late on long takes. Cutting on them lands mid-word.
- Speech-to-text hears "80 bucks" as "$80" and respells names. That is not an error. A missing or different word is.
- Voices mispronounce product names and read "212" as digits. Respell them for the voice and keep the on-screen text as written.
- Age-gated uploads cannot be fetched without a login. Use the open trailers, the maker's own site and official screenshots.
- Re-uploads carry another channel's watermark and end card. Check the channel name before you download.
- A card over a face or over text already in the footage looks broken. Move the card to the side or pin a different shot.
- If a cut lands a few frames from a card going up, the blur flickers. Move the cut onto the card's first frame.
- A caption that starts under a centred card collides with it. Put it below the card or end it when the card comes up.
- Exporting 9,000 transparent frames takes about 20 minutes for a 5-minute film. Render the preview first.
- A mock-up of a store page or a notification must be marked as one. A real capture gets a source pill.
- Say which rung every claim is on: official, reported, estimate, unknown. One wrong fact in public costs more than a missing one.
- This is commentary over quoted footage. Keep the source list, write the credits, and let me decide what gets published.
- Scene detection misses cuts inside a scene. Look at the first and last frame of every pinned shot, not just the middle one, or a caption lands on the wrong people.
- A screenshot of a short headline comes out as a small dark strip. If a headline card is under a third of the frame wide, set it as text on white instead.
</gotchas>

2. The viewer: who they are and what they are about to do.
3. The length: a 60-90 s sample, 5 minutes, or the full 20-35 minutes.
4. The voice: an ElevenLabs voice id and key if I have them, otherwise a free local voice. If it is paid, tell me the character count (about 1 credit each) and wait for my yes.

<direction>
A faceless 1920x1080, 30 fps explainer built entirely on real moving footage of the subject: official trailers, gameplay reveals, launch films, keynote clips, press b-roll, archive film. About 90% of the picture is that footage. There is no face-cam, no talking head, no AI-generated plate and no stock clip that is not the subject.
The picture changes about every 2 seconds, always with hard cuts, at the same rate from the first second to the last. Every concrete thing the voice names gets proof on screen inside half a second: a rounded glass card holding a photo, a real headline screenshot, a character panel, a typed quote or one big number. While a card is up, the footage keeps running behind it, blurred 26 px and darkened 40-60%.
One look for every graphic: dark plum glass #1E1322, a thin pale-pink border #F7D3EA with a soft pink glow (255,120,205), Montserrat Black in uppercase, and a left-to-right gradient #FF93DC to #FFB27C on captions, chapter words, numbers and names. Source pills are pink #FB96E6, cream #FFF1DE or peach #FFBA90 with dark caps. If the subject is not warm and neon, take two neighbouring hues from its key art and keep the panels near-black in the same hue.
The voice is fast, flat and plain. It says "you" constantly, marks every opinion as one, and names where each fact came from.
Banned: a greeting, a channel or narrator name, "in today's video", "let's dive in", a recap of what was just said, "thanks for watching", dissolves between shots, a subtitle for every word, a sound effect on cuts or text, music loud enough to notice, any shot shown twice, any shot over 6 s, a card over a face, a mock-up shown as a real screenshot, a leak used as evidence, and any fact with no named source.
</direction>

<structure>
Length and pace: 205-215 words a minute. 60-90 s is about 210-320 words; 5 minutes is about 1,050; 20 minutes is 4,300; 30 minutes is 6,400. The picture changes about 28 times a minute, 24-29 times in the first 60 s.
The shape: line 1 is a fact about the subject or a "you" line about the viewer's habit, with the first concrete fact inside 10 seconds → an intro of 30-65 s (110-230 words) holding one stakes line about the viewer, one scope promise ("everything" or a number), 3-6 teaser facts of one clause each, one trust line ("I checked every single thing") and one promise parked "at the very end" → a handoff of under 8 words that names section 1 → sections of 2:10-2:40 each (none under 0:55, none over 4:15; 10-13 of them in a full video, 2 in a 5-minute cut), ordered as a chain so each bridge can truthfully say "you now have X, so Y" → inside a section: open on old way vs new way or a one-word label, put the biggest change first, flag the most important item out loud in the middle ("and this is the big one"), end long sections with three actions in one sentence, then a 1-2 sentence bridge that states the next topic as a problem → every intro teaser is paid off later with a spoken callback ("remember the ___ from the start?"), never two payoffs in one section, the last one in the final 10% → the end promise is teased again between 20% and 40% of the way through → one subscribe ask between 30% and 50%, 2-4 sentences, joined by "because" to a tease of the next section → the close, under 60 s: a personal plan in three steps, "here's my hot take" in 3-4 sentences, "but you tell me" with an either/or question, then one sign-off line.
The fact unit, repeated every 15-25 s (about 57 words, 16 s): the claim in 1-2 sentences of 15 words or fewer → the named source in the same or next sentence ("X told Y", "X says", "you can see it in the trailer") → a confidence label if it is not official ("only X has reported it", "the reports don't agree yet", "nobody has shown that", "busted") → a line starting with "So" that says what you do, avoid or check → sometimes one joke, always after the fact, never two in a row.
The voice rules: sentences average 12-14 words, at least 28% of them 8 words or fewer, none over 50. At least 72% one-syllable words. "You" or "your" at least 8 times a minute, "I" 2-4 times, "we" almost never. 30-40% of sentences start with "And" or "So". A named source at least every 20 s, never 85 s without one. A "So" line at least every 30 s. Round every number with "about", say units the way people say them, and follow a big number with something the viewer knows ("about 210 gigs, a third of your console's drive"). Pick one piece of advice as the motif and say it at least 4 times, including in the last line.
</structure>

1. Tools (all free, all local). Install what's missing and tell me what you installed:
   - Python 3.10+ with numpy and Pillow, FFmpeg with ffprobe, yt-dlp
   - Playwright with Chromium, for headline screenshots and for drawing the graphics layer
   - faster-whisper with large-v3-turbo, int8 on the CPU, for word timings
   - Montserrat Black and Bold (free licence)
   - Kokoro (kokoro-onnx) for the free voice, or my ElevenLabs key read from a file and never printed
   - One project folder per video: research, script, a media folder with a source list, the voice, the timeline, the renders
2. Research, before any writing:
   - Search the web and open the pages. Nothing from memory.
   - For each fact keep the claim, the page, the exact words it rests on, the date and the confidence: official, on-record interview, seen by a previewer, single source, sources disagree, estimate, unknown, false.
   - Prefer the maker's own pages, then on-record interviews, then named outlets. Check every fact against a second source and drop what you cannot confirm.
   - You need one usable fact per 16 s of film, so about 19 for 5 minutes.
3. Script, then a check you run on it:
   - Write one sentence per line under section headings, and mark each teaser, payoff, joke, flag and the ask.
   - Write a small checker and run it until it passes: first fact inside 10 s, intro 30-65 s, every teaser paid off, mean sentence length 12-14 words, a named source every 20 s, "you" 8 times a minute, words per minute, one ask between 30% and 50%, none of the banned phrases.
   - Write out how the voice should say anything it will get wrong: product names, numbers, places ("212" as "two hundred and twelve").
   - Show me the script, the source list and the checker's result before you record.
4. Voice and timing:
   - Record one take per section, not per sentence: it flows better.
   - Transcribe each take with faster-whisper and match its words to the script with difflib. Take every time from that match, never from the voice service's own timestamps, which drift up to 0.4 s late on long takes.
   - List every word that was heard differently from the script. A name spelled another way is fine. A wrong word means redoing that one section only.
   - Cut silences down to 0.30 s, and only inside real silence (under -35 dB), keeping 35 ms either side. Then, if the pace is still under 205 wpm, speed up by at most 1.12x and stop there, even if it lands lower.
   - Level with a light compressor and two-pass loudnorm to -18 LUFS, loudness range 3 LU or less, true peak under -2 dB.
5. Media, with every file's page, link and date saved in one source list:
   - Footage: list the search results first and take the maker's own upload, never a re-upload with someone's watermark. 2-4 sources per 10 minutes of film.
   - Split each source into scenes with FFmpeg's scene score, make a numbered sheet of them, and look at it. Drop logos, title cards, rating boards, "presents" plates, burned-in dates and anything intimate or graphic.
   - Count the shots: you need about 25 different ones per minute. If you are short, add official stills as full-frame shots, 2.8 s each with a 3% push-in over 2.5 s, but keep them under about 10% of the runtime.
   - Crop letterboxed sources to fill the frame.
   - Headlines: screenshot the headline alone on the page's own background with Playwright. If the crop is not clean, set the headline as text on white with the outlet and the date.
   - Photos: the page's main image, free-licence sources first (the maker's press kit, Wikimedia Commons, NASA).
6. Timeline and graphics, every time keyed to a word in the script, never to a fixed second:
   - Footage: cut every 1.7-3.7 s (aim for 2.6 s), alternating bright and dark scenes. Wherever the voice names something you can see, pin that exact shot under the word. Cut mid-sentence, not on pauses.
   - Cards start 0.12 s before their word and fade in and out over 0.25 s. Holds: photo 2.6 s, headline 2.8 s, character 2.8 s, number 1.5 s, quote until 0.9 s after its last word. A card needs at least 1.2 s on screen. Aim for a card up 35-40% of the runtime.
   - Photo card: the image keeps its own shape, up to 44% of the frame wide (portrait up to 30% wide and 74% tall), tilted 1.4°, with a name pill on its lower-left corner, footage behind darkened 42%.
   - Headline card: 50% of the frame wide, tilted 1.1°, the outlet as a pill on its top-left corner, footage behind darkened 50%.
   - Character card: a 474x896 portrait panel at x 64.5% (or 10.5% on the left), photo on top, name in the gradient, two lines under it, over sharp footage with no darkening.
   - Quote card: from x 19% to 81% with its top at y 54%, a pink opening mark, the words typed one by one with the voice in white, then a pink attribution pill, footage behind darkened 55%.
   - Number card: one gradient figure 250 px tall, shrunk to fit 80% of the width, with a small spaced line under it.
   - Captions: only the 1-6 key words of a sentence, centred at y 80%, wrapped at 60% of the width. 116 px for 1-2 words, 106 px for 3, 92 px for 4-5, 80 px for 6. Each word fades in over 0.2 s on the moment it is spoken, the layout never shifts, and the phrase is gone at the next cut or 0.6 s after its last word. One about every 6-7 s in the intro and every 8-10 s later.
   - Chapter words: 1-3 words at 214 px, shrunk to fit 72% of the width, held 2 s over footage blurred and darkened 60%. One per section.
   - Source pills: 27 px caps, tilted a few degrees, stacked from the top-left corner (66 px in, 52 px down, 76 px apart), one the first time each source is named in a section. Use them for confidence too: REPORTED, ESTIMATE, BUSTED.
   - Never more than 5 s of bare footage in the first minute, or 7 s after it.
   - Draw all of this as one transparent HTML page, export it frame by frame with Playwright, and lay it over the footage in FFmpeg, switching the blur on and off on the exact frames a card starts and ends.
7. Render, measure and look:
   - Before any render, draw every shot in film order with its caption written on it, and read all of them. Fix every caption that sits on the wrong picture.
   - Render a 960x540 preview first. Pull 4 frames a second from the first minute and from two 30 s windows later, and read every sheet: cards on their word, captions building with the voice, no card over a face, nothing bare for too long.
   - Look at one full-size frame of each card type and fix the finish: border weight, glow, corner radius, type size, blur depth.
   - Render 1080p, then measure and show me the numbers next to these targets: 25-31 picture changes a minute, median shot 1.9-2.4 s, 3% or fewer shots over 6 s, a card up 35-40% of the time, stills under 10%, longest pause 0.5 s, -18 LUFS, voice and captions within 50 ms of each other at the end of the film.
   - Do at least three look-and-fix rounds, then give me the film, a phone copy under 25 MB, a credits list of every source, and an honest list of what still falls short.
</build>

<gotchas>
- A trailer is cut for mood, so its best shots are often the wrong picture for a factual line. Check every caption against the shot under it, or "in-game purchases" ends up over a love scene.
- A slower narrator makes the film longer, which empties the footage pool. Add shots or stills. Never let a shot come round twice.
- Stills creep up when footage is short. Past 10% of the runtime the film starts to feel like a slideshow.
- Voice services return word timestamps that drift late on long takes. Cutting on them lands mid-word.
- Speech-to-text hears "80 bucks" as "$80" and respells names. That is not an error. A missing or different word is.
- Voices mispronounce product names and read "212" as digits. Respell them for the voice and keep the on-screen text as written.
- Age-gated uploads cannot be fetched without a login. Use the open trailers, the maker's own site and official screenshots.
- Re-uploads carry another channel's watermark and end card. Check the channel name before you download.
- A card over a face or over text already in the footage looks broken. Move the card to the side or pin a different shot.
- If a cut lands a few frames from a card going up, the blur flickers. Move the cut onto the card's first frame.
- A caption that starts under a centred card collides with it. Put it below the card or end it when the card comes up.
- Exporting 9,000 transparent frames takes about 20 minutes for a 5-minute film. Render the preview first.
- A mock-up of a store page or a notification must be marked as one. A real capture gets a source pill.
- Say which rung every claim is on: official, reported, estimate, unknown. One wrong fact in public costs more than a missing one.
- This is commentary over quoted footage. Keep the source list, write the credits, and let me decide what gets published.
</gotchas>

TRANSCRIPT
A lawsuit could constrain new AI models if a court grants the restrictions sought by four nonprofits. The groups allege public-safety harms and violations of California unfair-competition law, asking a San Francisco court to freeze development or deployment at five AI firms. The defendants named are Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI. The plaintiffs include Public Citizen and the Alliance for Secure AI. No court has ruled on the allegations, and the requested freeze is not an existing ban.

AI-generated candidate impersonations can manipulate the information voters see. The European Commission’s proposed election guidance asks very large platforms and search engines to label deepfakes clearly, keep those labels attached when shared, and swiftly remove illegal candidate deepfakes. It also proposes testing recommendation algorithms for manipulation before national elections and publishing post-election risk reports. The draft consultation opened November tenth and closes November twenty-third. These are proposed guidelines under the Digital Services Act, not new binding rules, and the draft does not request deletion of lawful content.

Small AI developers need a way to test systems with regulatory supervision before putting them on the market. The European Commission has adopted binding common procedures for AI testing sandboxes, giving small businesses and start-ups priority and free regulatory guidance, apart from exceptional costs. Selection decisions normally come within three months of a complete application or call deadline. The regulation was adopted November tenth. Participation provides written proof and an exit report documenting the testing, not certification that the product complies. Member states must establish at least one sandbox by August second, twenty twenty-seven.

Calling restaurants or service providers is a practical task AI agents can take on for people. Meta says Muse can place calls to American businesses, citing cable companies, motor-vehicle departments and restaurants as examples. The feature previously served selected early adopters. It is now available to paid subscribers in the United States, an expansion of access rather than the first introduction of calling. TechCrunch reports that subscriptions start at twenty dollars a month; the report does not provide independent success-rate or business-acceptance figures.

AI-written clinical notes require checks before becoming part of a patient’s record. EkaCare says India’s National Health Authority selected it for an AI scribe that listens to consultations and creates structured notes in more than fifteen Indian languages, including mixed-language conversations. A verified doctor must review, edit if necessary, and approve every note before linkage to the patient account. The company also open-sourced Lipi, its related conversation-to-notes AI scribe framework, which individuals and organizations can run on their own infrastructure. The clinical system is designed for authority-controlled infrastructure and hospital-software integration; the announcement establishes neither national rollout nor measured clinical gains.

Using AI in education raises a concrete question: does a tool preserve the learner’s chances to practice skills and build human relationships? Harvard’s Compass Collaborative includes an AI Guidance by Age matrix that tailors recommendations to learner age, developmental domain and the user’s role. Researchers drew on more than five thousand education, psychology and development studies, much of it from before generative AI. The initiative launched November tenth. The matrix is an evolving advisory resource with assessment considerations and possible benefits or harms, while direct evidence of AI’s learning effects remains limited. It does not prove that a particular AI tool improves learning.

An AI-authorship accusation put a winning writer’s work and literary award under scrutiny. The Guardian reports that the Pangram detector rated the story as almost entirely AI-generated, which the author denied. The Caine Prize board interviewed the author, judges and publisher and commissioned independent metadata analysis of draft documents. The board found no evidence that generative AI produced the story and confirmed that the award stands. That is the prize’s review finding, not scientific validation of AI detectors. The prize also plans AI declarations for twenty twenty-seven submissions and shortlisted writers, judge guidance and a process for reviewing future concerns.

In 1949, Indian mathematician and schoolteacher D. R. Kaprekar uncovered one of arithmetic’s most fascinating numerical mysteries: 6174, now famously known as Kaprekar’s Constant.

The process is surprisingly simple. Choose any four-digit number containing at least two different digits, arrange its digits from largest to smallest and smallest to largest, then subtract the smaller number from the larger. Repeat the process with each result, keeping any leading zeros, and you’ll always reach 6174 in no more than seven steps.

What makes this number extraordinary is what happens next. Once you reach 6174, the process becomes an endless loop: 7641 − 1467 = 6174. No matter how many times you repeat it, the result never changes.

More than 75 years after its discovery, Kaprekar’s Constant continues to fascinate mathematicians and curious minds alike, revealing how something as simple as rearranging digits can uncover an astonishing mathematical pattern.

text:
Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

text:
Statement : Meta told the Home Ministry it acted against 61,000 posts in the fortnight after Chalo Sansad. IFF calls for the record to be made public.

New Delhi, 13 November 2026

Meta has told the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the cybercrime arm of the Ministry of Home Affairs, that it acted on more than 61,000 Facebook and Instagram posts it classified as violent and inciteful between 25 July and 7 August 2026, @ThePrintIndia reported on 12 November. That is about three posts a minute for 14 days. The period begins on the day the Education Minister resigned and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) ended its protest at Jantar Mantar, five days after police used tear gas and a lathi charge against its Chalo Sansad march.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the absence of any public account of this action. Meta disclosed the figure to the Home Ministry at a meeting on 21 August, and it became public only because the minutes were filed in the Supreme Court's suo motu proceedings on digital arrest scams.. In IFF's assessment, the minutes record direct pressure from the Ministry of Home Affairs on the content Meta carries.

As per the report in The Print a meeting was chaired by Rajesh Kumar, I4C's chief executive, and followed reviews by the Union Home Secretary, a parliamentary committee and a court-monitored committee on digital arrests. Its scope was wider than financial fraud. 

According to ThePrint, I4C sought an in-person briefing on "how the algorithm amplifies or suppresses specific content and viral accounts", an analysis of bot networks across prominent handles, and Meta's draft guidelines on deepfakes and re-uploaded content for review.
The minutes, as reported, do not state what the 61,000 posts concerned. It is not known which agency, if any, flagged them, or which law or company rule Meta applied. I4C itself did not accept aggregate figures when Meta cited 70 lakh pieces of content removed, it asked for examples with links. Users and the public are entitled to the same detail.

Complaints received by IFF show what was being restricted on Instagram as the period began. Here we are relying on our own inbound queries and requests for pro-bono help and legal assistance.

1) On 23 July, a story about the protests shared by a private account with 137 followers was made unavailable in India through what Instagram described as "an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements" under the IT Rules, 2021.

2) On 24 July, a reel by the journalist Ila Kazmi showing a Delhi Police facial recognition van scanning protesters at Jantar Mantar was withheld on a notice from "The Government of India / Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", which referred her to the Government of India for any questions. The Delhi High Court has directed the Home Ministry, the IT Ministry, the Delhi Police and Meta to produce the notice and will next hear the case on 17 November.

3) On 28 July, three days after the minister's resignation, Instagram withheld a video published on 15 June by the current-affairs page Unmutezone under the title "Why Modi Can't Ask Dharmendra Pradhan to Resign?". Its editor reported that a second video was blocked on 3 August.

Press reports describe similar restrictions. Newslaundry reported that an interview by the journalist Yaqut Ali with a former CJP spokesperson, posted on 26 July, was blocked in India within minutes, and that Facebook reels on the protests by the creator Jyoti Yadav, including an interview with AAP's Sanjay Singh, were restricted. It later reported restrictions on Instagram posts by Scroll and The Hindu about pellet-gun victims in Kashmir. None of this content is violent or inciteful, and Meta has not said whether it forms part of the figure.

The Home Ministry is involved at each stage from notices under Section 79(3)(b) reach platforms through the Sahyog portal, which I4C operates where close to 1.95 lakh blocking orders were issued to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026, most of them through the portal, and Meta has integrated its systems with it so that flagged content can be restricted without human review. On 27 July the Delhi Police, which reports to the Home Ministry, was reported to have directed platforms to remove posts it considered offensive to the Prime Minister. Meta's transparency report lists violence and incitement among the categories that I4C refers to it. A ministry that operates this channel and also reviews Meta's enforcement figures and algorithm is supervising online speech.

We regret to state that the Supreme Court's own proceedings have provided an avenue for such censorship without sufficient checks and balances. In the suo motu digital arrest case, in which it directed intermediaries to place their proposals before I4C, and in the Just Rights for Children Alliance matters, in which it indicated that platforms may lose safe harbour, the Court has largely acted as a facilitator of executive action rather than as an adjudicator of its constitutional limits. The objectives of curbing fraud and protecting children are legitimate, but the supervision they have enabled now extends to lawful speech and results in censorship without legal authority.

These restrictions do not have a basis in law and often executive rulemaking is being used to circumvent the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. Section 79(3)(b) sets a condition for a platform's immunity and in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court confined it to court orders and government notifications within Article 19(2). The power to block lies in Section 69A, which requires written reasons, committee review and, following Tanul Thakur (2022), a copy of the order and a hearing for the author. Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules requires each intimation to state reasons, the provision, the unlawful act and the URL, and to be reviewed monthly by a Secretary-rank officer. These requirements cannot be met through an automated integration with a three-hour deadline, whatever share of the 61,000 posts came through Sahyog.

Further, we state that while it may constitute a category of harmful speech, "Violent and inciteful" is not a ground for state mandated censorship under Article 19(2). Shreya Singhal protects discussion and advocacy and permits restriction only at the stage of incitement; a video asking why a minister has not resigned is discussion. Nor is there any clear statutory basis for I4C to perform the function of review a platform's content guidelines or to ask which accounts its algorithm promotes.

Our demands

1) The Ministry of Home Affairs must publish the minutes of its meetings with Meta in 2026 and state how many of the 61,000 posts were flagged by I4C, the Delhi Police or any other agency through Sahyog.

2) Meta must publish a breakdown of the 61,000 posts by the rule or law applied, the action taken and the requesting authority, and give each affected user the notice on which it acted. Further monthly breakdowns with qualitative disclosure is necesary.

3) I4C must withdraw its requests to review Meta's draft guidelines and to be briefed on its algorithm. Oversight of this kind requires a law made by Parliament and may only be performed by an independent regulatory body with a clear mandate and objective.

4) The Union Government must publish the monthly Secretary-level reviews under Rule 3(1)(d) for July and August 2026.

5) Meta must end the automatic execution of government and police flags in India and provide human review, a reasoned notice and an opportunity to respond before any restriction.

Users whose posts or accounts were restricted in India in July or August 2026 may write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots of each notice.
